title: Pass by value
learningGoals: show that the original does not change

youtube.title: C++ Pass by Value: Why Your Change Disappears | C++ Programming EP 23
youtube.description: In this episode you will explain that arguments are copied, show that the original does not change and return a result instead, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Pass by value · 0:47 A copy is changed · 1:27 Two separate boxes · 1:57 Second program · 2:57 Recap · 3:27 Bug of the Day · 4:15 Challenge · 4:35 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "A COPY!" in tomato on mint; Xecxec next to a photocopier making a copy of a box; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a photocopier making a copy of a box

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we meet a surprise. A function can change its input, and your variable still stays the same.

scenes.onScreen: "Pass by value": numbered lines (1. The function gets a copy of the argument; 2. Changes to the copy stay inside; 3. Return the result to send it out) and an analogy card: a photocopy: you scribble on the copy, and the original stays clean
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: When you pass a value to a function, C plus plus makes a copy. The function works on the copy. The original variable never changes. This is called pass by value. To send a result out, use return. Think of a photocopy. You can scribble on the copy, and the original stays clean.
points: The function gets a copy of the argument
Changes to the copy stay inside
Return the result to send it out

analogy.title: Pass by value
analogy.body: A photocopy: you scribble on the copy, and the original stays clean

scenes.onScreen: copy.cpp: double_it changes its own copy
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 10] Number is ten. [HL 11] We call double it with number. C plus plus copies ten into the parameter n. [HL 5] The function doubles its copy. [HL 6] Inside the function, n is twenty. [HL 12] Back in main, number is still ten. The copy was changed, not the original.

scenes.onScreen: memory boxes: number in main and n in double_it have different addresses
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in one by one with size and address tags; arrows draw on as the narrator mentions them; regions are labelled; pop per box
scenes.narration: Look at the two boxes. Number lives in main. N lives in the function. They have different addresses. The function doubled n to twenty. The box named number still holds ten.

scenes.onScreen: noswap.cpp: swap_values swaps copies, not the originals
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 4] The function swaps a and b. [HL 5] It uses a helper box t. [HL 12] Main calls it with x and y. The function swaps only its copies. [HL 13] So x is still one, and y is still two. We need another way to change the originals. That is the next episode.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as noswap dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints one and two. Nothing was swapped.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. Arguments are copied into the parameters. Two. A change to the copy does not reach the original. Three. Use return to send a result out. Four. Next episode: references change the original. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: Arguments are copied into the parameters.
A change to the copy does not reach the original.
Use return to send a result out.
Next episode: references change the original.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Expecting the original to change
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the program runs and the wrong output appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the output turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. Add tax should raise the price to one hundred and five. But the program prints one hundred. The function changed only a copy. Return the new price, and store it in the variable. Now the answer is right.

scenes.onScreen: I gave my function a copy of my homework. It said, nice try, I will only change the copy.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: I gave my function a copy of my homework. It said, nice try, I will only change the copy.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: predict the output before you run
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a function that adds one to its int parameter. Call it from main. Print the variable before and after. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: pass by reference. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Program output (it runs, but the answer is wrong):

Price: 100
bug.why: The function changes its own copy of price, and then the copy disappears. Return the new value and store it in the variable.

pun: "I gave my function a copy of my homework. It said, nice try, I will only change the copy."
challenge: Write a function that adds one to its int parameter. Call it from main. Print the variable before and after.
challengeAnswer: The variable does not change, because the function adds one to a copy. To change it, return the new value and store it.
